recommendations.duration: 5–7 days depending on regimen

recommendations.label: Moderate to severe
preferred: Benzylpenicillin 1.5 million units IV q6h
alternative: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h
recommendations.duration: 7 days
notes: HPUSM source states to add steroid for all severe leptospirosis.

recommendations.label: Severe disease
preferred: Benzylpenicillin 1.5 million units IV q6h OR ceftriaxone 1 g IV q12h
recommendations.duration: 7 days
notes: MSIC source states there is insufficient evidence to support routine corticosteroids in pulmonary haemorrhage.

recommendations.label: Mild disease
preferred: Azithromycin 500 mg PO q24h for 3 days OR doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h for 5–7 days OR amoxicillin 500 mg PO q8h for 7 days
recommendations.duration: Regimen-specific

recommendations.label: Mild adult disease
preferred: Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h for 5–7 days OR amoxicillin 500 mg PO q8h for 7 days
alternative: Azithromycin 500 mg PO q24h for 3 days; amoxicillin/azithromycin are pregnancy options in the NAG pathway
recommendations.duration: 5–7 days depending on regimen.

recommendations.label: Moderate / severe adult disease
preferred: Benzylpenicillin 1.5 million units IV q6h
alternative: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h
recommendations.duration: 7–10 days; corticosteroids are not routine solely for leptospirosis.

why: The source conflict on corticosteroid use is deliberately not reconciled by the app.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Spirochaetal dissemination and endothelial/organ injury can cause AKI, jaundice, bleeding and pulmonary disease.
diagnosticMicrobiology: PCR is most useful early; IgM/MAT serology becomes useful later. Culture is slow and not used for urgent treatment decisions.

conditions.name: Lung Abscess / Empyema
conditions.summary: Antibiotics are only one component; drainage/source control is central when a pleural collection is present.
before: Obtain appropriate cultures before antimicrobials when this does not cause harmful delay
Review previous microbiology and recent antimicrobial exposure
Check allergy and previous serious antimicrobial adverse reactions
Check renal function and whether renal replacement therapy is being used
Obtain pleural fluid/pus culture where feasible
Arrange drainage for empyema/complicated collection

recommendations.label: Local lung abscess
preferred: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q6–8h
alternative: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h + metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: 28–42 days in the source; step down when clinically improved

recommendations.label: Healthcare-associated aspiration/lung abscess
preferred: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g q6h OR cefepime 2 g q8h + metronidazole 500 mg q8h
alternative: Meropenem 1 g q8h OR imipenem 500 mg q6h
recommendations.duration: Lung abscess minimum 4 weeks; response/imaging dependent

recommendations.label: No recent thoracic procedure or HAP/VAP
preferred: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q6–8h OR ampicillin–sulbactam 3 g IV q6h
alternative: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h + metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
β-lactam allergy: clindamycin 600 mg IV/PO q8h
recommendations.duration: After adequate source control: generally 2–4 weeks from drainage/surgery and defervescence; longer (4–6 weeks) if source control is inadequate.

recommendations.label: Post-procedure / concomitant HAP-VAP
preferred: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6–8h OR cefepime 2 g IV q8h + metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h; add vancomycin when indicated
alternative: Meropenem 1 g IV q8h; add vancomycin when indicated
recommendations.duration: Source-control dependent; generally 2–6 weeks.

conditions.diseaseMechanism: Microbial infection of airways/alveoli triggers local inflammatory exudate and impaired gas exchange; aspiration, ventilation, host defence and resistance risk determine likely pathogens.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain a quality respiratory specimen for microscopy/culture when disease is severe, hospital-acquired or treatment failure/MDR is a concern.
Blood cultures are appropriate in severe/systemic illness; interpret respiratory growth with colonisation risk and clinical/radiologic findings.

conditions.name: Melioidosis
conditions.summary: MSIC describes a prolonged two-phase treatment strategy: an IV intensive phase followed by oral eradication therapy, with duration determined by infection site and severity.
before: Obtain cultures; culture is the diagnostic mainstay
Look for deep-seated abscesses and consider CT/ultrasound abdomen/pelvis in culture-positive disease
Assess need for drainage or surgical intervention
Check renal function and TMP-SMX contraindications/interactions

recommendations.label: Initial intensive phase
preferred: Meropenem 1 g IV q8h (2 g q8h for CNS infection) OR imipenem 500 mg IV q6h
alternative: Ceftazidime 2 g IV q6h
recommendations.duration: At least 2 weeks; longer for pneumonia with ICU admission/bacteraemia, deep collections, osteomyelitis, CNS or arterial infection.
notes: Optional TMP-SMX is added in selected sites such as cutaneous disease, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, CNS infection and deep collections in the cited guide.

recommendations.label: Duration framework
preferred: Intensive-phase duration and eradication-phase duration are site-specific; the cited table ranges from 2 to 8 weeks intensive therapy and 3 to 6 months eradication therapy for many listed foci.
recommendations.duration: Use the site-specific melioidosis duration table.

recommendations.label: Intensive phase — mild/moderate non-neurological
preferred: Ceftazidime 2 g IV q6h
alternative: Escalate to a carbapenem regimen for severe disease, persistent bacteraemia or another source-specified indication.
recommendations.duration: At least 14 days IV; site/severity-specific intensive phase may be longer before eradication therapy.

recommendations.label: Severe sepsis / persistent bacteraemia
preferred: Meropenem 1 g IV q8h OR imipenem/cilastatin 500 mg IV q6h (higher source-listed dosing may be used for severe infection according to patient/context).
alternative: Once clinically improved, de-escalation to ceftazidime may be considered when appropriate.
recommendations.duration: Intensive phase is prolonged and site/severity dependent; do not shorten below the source-required minimum.

recommendations.label: Neuromelioidosis / ICU septic shock with augmented renal clearance
preferred: Meropenem 2 g IV q8h
alternative: Add trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole for selected neurological, osteoarticular, genitourinary/prostatic, skin/soft-tissue, ocular, testicular or pericardial foci according to the NAG pathway.
recommendations.duration: Use the NAG site-specific intensive-phase duration, then complete eradication therapy; ID consultation is strongly appropriate for severe/complex disease.

why: Severe disease, deep infection and CNS/vascular involvement require longer treatment than uncomplicated infection.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Environmental inoculation/inhalation/ingestion can lead to pneumonia, sepsis and multiple deep abscesses; intracellular persistence explains relapse risk and the need for eradication therapy.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Culture appropriate specimens (blood plus site-specific samples); alert the laboratory when melioidosis is suspected.

sourceReconciliation.title: Melioidosis — Jan 2026 current NAG update vs MSIC ICU
sourceReconciliation.summary: The live NAG melioidosis section was updated in January 2026 and is treated as the freshness authority for the national pathway; the MSIC ICU guide remains an ICU reference layer.
points: Current NAG intensive therapy distinguishes mild/moderate non-neurological disease (ceftazidime) from severe disease (meropenem or imipenem).
Current NAG specifically lists meropenem 2 g IV q8h for neuromelioidosis and for septic shock requiring ICU support with augmented renal clearance.
Intensive and eradication durations are site-specific; deep abscesses and source control/drainage must be assessed.

conditions.name: Necrotising Fasciitis
conditions.summary: Surgical source control is time-critical. Antimicrobials should not delay debridement.
before: Urgent surgical review and debridement/source control
Blood cultures and deep operative tissue cultures
Assess shock and organ support requirements

recommendations.label: Local empirical regimen
preferred: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6–8h ± clindamycin 600–900 mg IV q8h
alternative: Ampicillin–sulbactam 3 g IV q6h
recommendations.duration: 7–14 days in the source; tailor to source control and clinical response

recommendations.label: National source-control principle
preferred: Immediate aggressive surgical debridement is the primary treatment; empirical antimicrobial therapy should be broad and then streamlined to intraoperative culture and susceptibility.
recommendations.duration: Duration is source- and response-dependent after adequate debridement.
notes: Repeated debridement may be required for source control.

conditions.diseaseMechanism: Organisms breach skin/soft-tissue barriers and trigger local inflammation; deep fascial spread, toxin production, ischemia and impaired host defence drive severe disease.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Superficial swabs are often low yield; obtain deep tissue/pus or operative specimens in severe, necrotising, diabetic-foot or treatment-failure disease.
Blood cultures are appropriate when systemic toxicity, severe immunocompromise or bacteraemia is suspected.

conditions.name: Osteomyelitis
conditions.summary: HPUSM separates acute empirical treatment from chronic disease, where surgical debridement and tissue culture guide therapy.
before: Obtain appropriate deep/tissue cultures where feasible
Assess for surgical debridement/source control
Review prior microbiology, implants and chronicity

recommendations.label: Acute osteomyelitis
preferred: Cloxacillin 2 g IV q6h
alternative: Clindamycin 600 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: 2–4 weeks IV followed by oral therapy; total 6 weeks in the source table.

recommendations.label: Chronic osteomyelitis
preferred: Empirical treatment is not indicated; surgical debridement and tissue culture/susceptibility guide treatment.
recommendations.duration: Source table lists 6 weeks to 3 months depending on context.

recommendations.label: Acute osteomyelitis
preferred: Cloxacillin 2 g IV q6h; tailor to tissue/bone culture
alternative: Cefazolin 2 g IV q6–8h for appropriate β-lactam allergy context
recommendations.duration: Initial IV 2–4 weeks then oral therapy; minimum total 6 weeks, modified by response. S. aureus osteomyelitis with bacteraemia requires prolonged IV therapy.

why: Chronic osteomyelitis is a source-control and culture-directed problem rather than an empirical-antibiotic-only problem.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Infection reaches bone/joint by haematogenous spread, contiguous extension, trauma/procedure or prosthetic biofilm; devascularised tissue and foreign material reduce antimicrobial efficacy.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain bone/joint/deep tissue or aspirate cultures before definitive antibiotics when clinically safe.
Blood cultures are important for haematogenous disease; imaging defines extent/source-control needs.

conditions.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia
conditions.summary: MSIC ICU provides pathogen-specific therapy for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in severe community-acquired pneumonia pathways.
before: Confirm immunocompromised context and obtain appropriate diagnostic specimens where feasible
Check renal function, potassium and blood counts before high-dose trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole
Assess whether adjunctive corticosteroid criteria are met

recommendations.label: Preferred
preferred: Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole 5 mg/kg (TMP component) IV q6–8h
alternative: Pentamidine 4 mg/kg IV daily OR primaquine 30 mg PO q24h PLUS clindamycin 600–900 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: 21 days

recommendations.label: Adult HIV-associated PJP/PCP — national pathway
preferred: Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole 15–20 mg/kg/day (TMP component) IV/PO in 3–4 divided doses
alternative: Mild–moderate: clindamycin 600 mg IV/PO q8h + primaquine 30 mg base PO q24h; severe: pentamidine 4 mg/kg/day IV OR clindamycin + primaquine
recommendations.duration: 21 days; severe disease should receive adjunctive corticosteroid according to the NAG regimen.
notes: Consider IV→PO switch after clinical improvement because trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole and clindamycin have high oral bioavailability.
Check G6PD status before dapsone or primaquine.

why: High-dose TMP-SMX is weight-based on the trimethoprim component and requires toxicity monitoring.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: P. jirovecii proliferates in alveoli of immunocompromised hosts, producing diffuse interstitial/alveolar inflammation and severe gas-exchange impairment.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Induced sputum or BAL with PCR/microscopy is typical; serum β-D-glucan can support but is not organism-specific.

conditions.name: Postpartum Endometritis
conditions.summary: Treat postpartum uterine infection with broad polymicrobial coverage and reassess for retained products/abscess if response is poor.
before: Obtain cultures when clinically indicated
Assess retained products and source-control need

recommendations.label: Empirical postpartum endometritis
preferred: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.2 g IV q8h OR ampicillin/sulbactam 3 g IV q6h
alternative: Cefotaxime 1 g IV q8h + metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h + gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV once
OR clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h + gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV q24h
recommendations.duration: Continue IV until clinically improved (including resolution of fundal tenderness) and afebrile for 24–48 h. If an oral regimen is subsequently administered, NAG lists 14 days total oral-regimen duration.
notes: TDM is required for ongoing gentamicin therapy. Reassess for retained products/abscess or another source if response is poor.

why: Failure to improve should trigger evaluation for retained products, abscess or another diagnosis.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Infection causes tissue injury through organism-specific invasion/toxin effects and the host inflammatory response; severity depends on pathogen, site, inoculum, source control and host reserve.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain microbiological specimens from the suspected source before antibiotics when this can be done without unsafe delay.
Interpret culture/PCR results with syndrome, host factors, prior antimicrobials and colonisation/contamination risk.

conditions.name: Prosthetic Joint Infection
conditions.summary: Do not start routine empirical therapy before adequate cultures in a stable patient; treatment is culture- and surgical-strategy dependent.
before: Withhold empirical antibiotics in stable patient until appropriate specimens are obtained
Define surgical strategy: DAIR vs one-/two-stage revision/removal
Obtain multiple deep tissue cultures

recommendations.label: Culture-directed principle
preferred: Empirical treatment is not recommended before specimens; MSSA pathway uses cloxacillin + rifampicin when implant remains; MRSA pathway uses vancomycin + rifampicin.
alternative: Follow susceptibility and surgical plan.
recommendations.duration: Surgical strategy and organism determine duration.

recommendations.label: National culture-directed principle
preferred: Empirical treatment is generally not recommended before adequate cultures in stable prosthetic-joint infection.
alternative: For susceptible staphylococci with retained implant, rifampicin-containing combinations are used in source-specific pathways.
recommendations.duration: Typically prolonged and surgery-dependent; check current NAG orthopaedic section.

conditions.diseaseMechanism: Infection reaches bone/joint by haematogenous spread, contiguous extension, trauma/procedure or prosthetic biofilm; devascularised tissue and foreign material reduce antimicrobial efficacy.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain bone/joint/deep tissue or aspirate cultures before definitive antibiotics when clinically safe.
Blood cultures are important for haematogenous disease; imaging defines extent/source-control needs.

conditions.name: Pyogenic Liver Abscess
conditions.summary: Antimicrobial therapy must be paired with drainage/source control when indicated; sepsis shifts empiric breadth.
before: Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics when feasible
Obtain aspirate/drainage culture when procedure performed
Assess abscess size and need for drainage
Assess sepsis/organ failure and prior biliary instrumentation

recommendations.label: Non-sepsis
preferred: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q6h OR ampicillin–sulbactam 3 g IV q6h
alternative: Cefoperazone, ceftriaxone, cefotaxime or cefuroxime ± metronidazole according to anaerobic risk
recommendations.duration: 2–6 weeks; shorter with adequate drainage and fever resolution; step down when improving.

recommendations.label: Sepsis / organ failure
preferred: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6–8h
alternative: Use source-specific alternatives and resistance-risk assessment
recommendations.duration: 2–6 weeks; source-control dependent. q8h piperacillin–tazobactam is extended over 3–4 h.

why: Drainage/source control can shorten therapy and is part of definitive management.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Barrier disruption, obstruction, perforation or infected fluid collections expose normally sterile sites to enteric organisms; source control is a major determinant of cure.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Prioritise source-control imaging/procedure where indicated and culture normally sterile intra-abdominal/biliary/abscess material when obtained.
Blood cultures are useful in sepsis; avoid overinterpreting cultures from chronically placed drains.

conditions.name: Rickettsial Infection
conditions.summary: Doxycycline is the key first-line therapy for typical rickettsial disease; severe illness may require combination/source-specific treatment.
before: Review exposure/travel and organ dysfunction
Send appropriate serology/PCR when available without delaying treatment in strongly suspected severe disease

recommendations.label: Mild rickettsial disease
preferred: Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h for 5 days
alternative: Azithromycin 500 mg PO q24h for 3 days; NAG uses azithromycin in pregnancy.
recommendations.duration: 5 days doxycycline or 3 days azithromycin in the listed mild regimen.

recommendations.label: Moderate–severe disease / organ involvement
preferred: Azithromycin 500 mg IV q12h on day 1 then 500 mg IV q24h for 6 days PLUS doxycycline 200 mg PO q12h on day 1 then 100 mg PO q12h for 6 days
recommendations.duration: Source-listed 7-day severe regimen; switch IV to PO once clinically improved and able to absorb oral medication.
notes: Severe features include ARDS/shock, myocarditis, meningoencephalitis, hepatitis or renal failure.

why: Clinical response to doxycycline can be rapid, but severe organ involvement still requires ICU support and diagnostic confirmation.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Infection causes tissue injury through organism-specific invasion/toxin effects and the host inflammatory response; severity depends on pathogen, site, inoculum, source control and host reserve.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain microbiological specimens from the suspected source before antibiotics when this can be done without unsafe delay.
Interpret culture/PCR results with syndrome, host factors, prior antimicrobials and colonisation/contamination risk.

conditions.name: Septic Arthritis
conditions.summary: Drainage/washout and culture-directed therapy are central; empirical therapy primarily targets S. aureus/streptococci in typical native-joint disease.
before: Obtain joint aspirate for cell count, Gram stain and culture before antibiotics if this does not delay urgent care
Obtain blood cultures in systemic illness
Arrange drainage/washout when indicated

recommendations.label: Native joint empirical — no specific Gram-negative risk
preferred: Cloxacillin 2 g IV q4–6h
alternative: Cefazolin 2 g IV q6–8h; clindamycin or vancomycin may be used in selected allergy/MRSA contexts
recommendations.duration: Typically 2–4 weeks IV then oral to complete 4–6 weeks, modified by organism/source control/response.

conditions.diseaseMechanism: Infection reaches bone/joint by haematogenous spread, contiguous extension, trauma/procedure or prosthetic biofilm; devascularised tissue and foreign material reduce antimicrobial efficacy.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain bone/joint/deep tissue or aspirate cultures before definitive antibiotics when clinically safe.
Blood cultures are important for haematogenous disease; imaging defines extent/source-control needs.

conditions.name: Septic Shock — Undifferentiated Empirical Antibiotic
conditions.summary: Use this only as an undifferentiated local starting reference. The final empirical regimen should be driven by suspected source, previous cultures, recent antibiotics and local resistance patterns.
before: Obtain blood cultures before antimicrobials if this does not delay treatment
Identify likely source and source control requirement
Review prior cultures/colonisation and recent antibiotics
Assess allergy, renal function and local resistance patterns

recommendations.label: Non-diabetic — undifferentiated local guide
preferred: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q8h
alternative: Source-directed therapy may supersede this
recommendations.duration: Revise/de-escalate at 48–72 h based on cultures and clinical source

recommendations.label: Diabetic — undifferentiated local guide
preferred: Ceftazidime 2 g IV q6–8h
alternative: Source-directed therapy may supersede this
recommendations.duration: Revise/de-escalate at 48–72 h

recommendations.label: Sepsis / septic shock — source-directed national principle
preferred: Give broad-spectrum empirical therapy directed at the most likely source and pathogens; incorporate prior microbiology, resistance risk/colonisation and local susceptibility data.
alternative: If source becomes apparent, switch to the source-specific NAG pathway rather than maintaining an undifferentiated regimen.
recommendations.duration: Reassess daily; modify/de-escalate at 48–72 h as microbiology and clinical trajectory clarify the diagnosis.

why: The MSIC ICU guide stresses rapid microbiological sampling, appropriate empirical coverage, PK/PD optimisation, source control and de-escalation.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Infection triggers a dysregulated host response with vasoplegia, endothelial/microcirculatory dysfunction and organ hypoperfusion; source control and timely effective antimicrobials are essential alongside resuscitation.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain microbiological specimens from the suspected source before antibiotics when this can be done without unsafe delay.
Interpret culture/PCR results with syndrome, host factors, prior antimicrobials and colonisation/contamination risk.

sourceReconciliation.title: Undifferentiated septic shock — local simplified table vs current NAG framework
sourceReconciliation.summary: HPUSM contains a simplified undifferentiated local table stratified by diabetes, whereas current NAG does not use diabetes alone as the principal selector for an empirical sepsis regimen.
points: Current NAG says empirical therapy should be source-directed whenever the source is apparent.

If the source is not apparent, current NAG says to incorporate age, acquisition setting, recent microbiology, drug-resistance/colonisation risk, local susceptibility, immune status and locally endemic exposures.
AbxHub therefore displays the HPUSM local table as its own source card and does not synthesize it into a universal “diabetic vs non-diabetic” rule.

conditions.name: Severe Community-Acquired Pneumonia
conditions.summary: Severe CAP requires severity assessment, atypical coverage when appropriate, and escalation to antipseudomonal therapy only when Pseudomonas risk is present.
before: Obtain appropriate cultures before antimicrobials when this does not cause harmful delay
Review previous microbiology and recent antimicrobial exposure
Check allergy and previous serious antimicrobial adverse reactions
Check renal function and whether renal replacement therapy is being used
Assess CAP severity (e.g. CURB-65/SMART-COP) and ICU need
Assess strong Pseudomonas risk and recent healthcare/antibiotic exposure

recommendations.label: Severe pneumonia (CURB65 >3)
preferred: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6–8h when Pseudomonas risk + azithromycin 500 mg IV/PO q24h
alternative: Use syndrome-/risk-specific alternative from local guidance
recommendations.duration: 5–7 days

recommendations.label: Severe CAP — usual pathogens
preferred: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q8h + azithromycin 500 mg IV q24h
alternative: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV q12h OR cefotaxime 2 g IV q8h + levofloxacin/moxifloxacin
recommendations.duration: Usually 5–7 days for β-lactam component; atypical duration varies

recommendations.label: If Pseudomonas risk
preferred: Cefepime 2 g IV q8h
alternative: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h
recommendations.duration: 7 days

recommendations.label: Severe CAP — national 2026-updated pathway
preferred: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q8h; may add azithromycin 500 mg IV/PO q24h for 3 days or doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h when atypical coverage is indicated
alternative: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h
If Pseudomonas risk: piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6–8h OR cefepime 2 g IV q8h
recommendations.duration: Usual severe CAP 5–7 days; antipseudomonal regimen 7 days.

why: Current NAG also emphasizes local antibiogram and pseudomonal risk before antipseudomonal therapy; open the live NAG page for the latest national wording.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Severe community-acquired pneumonia results from lower-respiratory invasion with intense host inflammatory response; pathogen spectrum changes with structural lung disease, post-influenza disease and other risk factors.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain a quality respiratory specimen for microscopy/culture when disease is severe, hospital-acquired or treatment failure/MDR is a concern.
Blood cultures are appropriate in severe/systemic illness; interpret respiratory growth with colonisation risk and clinical/radiologic findings.

sourceReconciliation.title: Severe CAP — HPUSM vs MSIC vs current NAG
sourceReconciliation.summary: The three sources agree that severity and Pseudomonas risk matter, but they frame the default severe-CAP regimen differently. AbxHub therefore keeps each regimen separate.
points: Current NAG (Jan 2026-updated severe CAP): amoxicillin/clavulanate is the preferred base regimen; atypical coverage is added when indicated, and antipseudomonal therapy is reserved for Pseudomonas risk.
MSIC ICU similarly uses amoxicillin/clavulanate plus atypical coverage for severe CAP and provides separate Pseudomonas-risk options.
HPUSM local guide lists piperacillin/tazobactam plus azithromycin for severe pneumonia when Pseudomonas risk applies.

conditions.name: Severe Malaria
conditions.summary: Parenteral artesunate is the preferred severe-malaria therapy in the MSIC source, with species-specific follow-on/eradication therapy.
before: Confirm parasitaemia/species where possible but do not delay severe-malaria treatment
Check glucose, haemolysis, renal and neurologic complications
Review pregnancy and G6PD status before species-specific adjuncts such as primaquine

recommendations.label: Severe malaria
preferred: Artesunate 2.4 mg/kg IV at 0, 12 and 24 h, then q24h while parenteral therapy remains required
alternative: Quinine dihydrochloride 20 mg/kg IV loading over 4 h, then 10 mg/kg q8h when artesunate is unavailable, with the source-listed companion therapy
recommendations.duration: Transition to oral ACT when clinically able; complete species-specific therapy.

why: Severe malaria is a time-critical multisystem emergency; antimalarial treatment runs in parallel with organ support.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: High parasite biomass, haemolysis, microvascular sequestration and host inflammatory responses drive multiorgan dysfunction in severe malaria.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Urgent thick/thin blood films or validated rapid diagnostic testing with parasite density; repeat testing if suspicion remains high.

conditions.name: Spinal Epidural Abscess
conditions.summary: Urgent diagnosis, source control/neurosurgical assessment and prolonged pathogen-directed therapy are required.
before: Obtain appropriate microbiology before antimicrobial therapy when this will not cause harmful delay
Review previous cultures and recent antimicrobial exposure
Check allergy, renal function and interacting/toxic co-medications
Assess source control and severity
Urgent MRI and surgical/neurosurgical assessment when neurological compromise or drainable collection is suspected

recommendations.label: Empirical staphylococcal coverage
preferred: Cloxacillin 2 g IV q6h
alternative: Add/replace with vancomycin when MRSA risk is important or the patient deteriorates
recommendations.duration: Usually ≥6 weeks; NAG notes at least an initial IV phase, modified by source control and response.

why: Neurological deterioration and inadequate source control can produce irreversible harm.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Pathogens invade the CNS or adjacent structures, generating inflammation within a confined compartment where oedema, vascular injury and raised intracranial pressure can cause neurologic damage.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain bone/joint/deep tissue or aspirate cultures before definitive antibiotics when clinically safe.
Blood cultures are important for haematogenous disease; imaging defines extent/source-control needs.

conditions.name: Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis
conditions.summary: Ascitic-fluid infection in cirrhosis. Diagnostic paracentesis, cultures and early therapy are central; distinguish primary SBP from secondary peritonitis.
before: Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic cell count/differential
Inoculate ascitic fluid into blood culture bottles at bedside when possible
Obtain blood cultures in septic patients
Assess for secondary peritonitis/source-control features

recommendations.label: Primary SBP — national pathway
preferred: Cefotaxime 2 g IV q8h OR ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h
alternative: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q6h OR ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q12h
recommendations.duration: 5–7 days; IV→PO ciprofloxacin may be considered when clinically appropriate.

recommendations.label: ICU principle
preferred: Treat when ascitic PMN count is ≥250 cells/mm³ in the appropriate clinical context; bedside inoculation into blood culture bottles improves culture yield.
recommendations.duration: Tailor to response and microbiology.

why: A positive culture is not required to start therapy when the clinical/ascitic neutrophil criteria support SBP.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Infection causes tissue injury through organism-specific invasion/toxin effects and the host inflammatory response; severity depends on pathogen, site, inoculum, source control and host reserve.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Prioritise source-control imaging/procedure where indicated and culture normally sterile intra-abdominal/biliary/abscess material when obtained.
Blood cultures are useful in sepsis; avoid overinterpreting cultures from chronically placed drains.

conditions.name: Suspected HSV Encephalitis
conditions.summary: Treat suspected HSV encephalitis promptly while diagnostic CSF/PCR and neuroimaging evaluation proceeds.
before: Obtain CSF/PCR when safe without delaying therapy
Check renal function and weight used for acyclovir dosing
Review need for neuroimaging before lumbar puncture

recommendations.label: Empirical HSV coverage
preferred: Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h
alternative: Adjust interval for renal impairment
recommendations.duration: Usually 14–21 days; use virologic/clinical response and specialist guidance.

why: Acyclovir is time-critical when HSV encephalitis is suspected; renal adjustment is central to safe therapy.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Pathogens invade the CNS or adjacent structures, generating inflammation within a confined compartment where oedema, vascular injury and raised intracranial pressure can cause neurologic damage.
diagnosticMicrobiology: CSF PCR is central for HSV/VZV and selected viral pathogens; MRI/EEG support the diagnosis.

conditions.name: Systemic Brucellosis
conditions.summary: Combination therapy is required to reduce relapse; focal disease and pregnancy require modified regimens.
before: Confirm occupational/food/animal exposure
Obtain blood cultures/serology and assess focal complications including endocarditis/neurobrucellosis

recommendations.label: Systemic disease
preferred: Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h × 6 weeks + gentamicin 5 mg/kg/day for the initial 7 days
alternative: Streptomycin 1 g IM daily for 2–3 weeks can replace gentamicin in a source-listed regimen; rifampicin-containing alternatives exist
recommendations.duration: Combination therapy commonly 6 weeks; focal disease is longer.

why: Monotherapy carries a higher relapse risk.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Infection causes tissue injury through organism-specific invasion/toxin effects and the host inflammatory response; severity depends on pathogen, site, inoculum, source control and host reserve.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Blood cultures and serology are commonly used; notify the laboratory because Brucella poses an occupational aerosol hazard.

conditions.name: Tetanus
conditions.summary: Management combines wound debridement, toxin neutralisation, antimicrobial therapy and intensive supportive control of spasms/autonomic dysfunction.
before: Immediate wound assessment/debridement
Administer tetanus immune globulin and initiate active immunisation as indicated
Prepare airway/autonomic supportive care for severe disease

recommendations.label: Adult tetanus — antimicrobial + toxin management
preferred: Metronidazole 500 mg IV q6–8h for 7–10 days
PLUS human tetanus immunoglobulin 500 IU IM once
PLUS age-appropriate anti-tetanus toxoid vaccine IM at a different site
alternative: Benzylpenicillin 100,000–200,000 units/kg/day IV divided q6h for 7–10 days, with the same immunoglobulin and active immunisation measures
recommendations.duration: 7–10 days antimicrobial therapy.
notes: Notifiable disease. Wound debridement is essential to eradicate spores/necrotic tissue. IV→PO switch may be considered once clinically improved where an appropriate oral regimen is available.

why: Antibiotics stop bacterial proliferation but do not neutralise toxin already bound to neural tissue.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: C. tetani spores germinate in devitalised anaerobic tissue; tetanospasmin blocks inhibitory neurotransmitter release, causing rigidity and autonomic instability.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Diagnosis is clinical; culture is insensitive and a negative wound culture does not exclude tetanus.

conditions.name: Toxoplasma Encephalitis
conditions.summary: Use a complete anti-toxoplasma combination regimen and treat long enough for clinical/radiologic response.
before: Confirm HIV/immunocompromised context
Review brain imaging and differential diagnosis
Check marrow/renal baseline before folate-antagonist therapy

recommendations.label: Preferred source-listed options
preferred: Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole using TMP 10 mg/kg/day divided q12h OR pyrimethamine-based combination + folinic acid + sulfadiazine
alternative: Clindamycin-containing alternative when sulfadiazine cannot be used
recommendations.duration: At least 6 weeks, then secondary prophylaxis according to host response.

why: Combination therapy and folinic acid rescue are integral to the pyrimethamine regimen.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Pathogens invade the CNS or adjacent structures, generating inflammation within a confined compartment where oedema, vascular injury and raised intracranial pressure can cause neurologic damage.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Brain imaging plus host risk profile and Toxoplasma serology support presumptive diagnosis; tissue diagnosis is considered when atypical/non-responsive.

conditions.name: Typhoid Fever
conditions.summary: Use susceptibility testing and local resistance data; XDR disease changes treatment.
before: Obtain cultures before therapy when feasible
Assess severity and complications
Review travel/exposure and resistance/susceptibility

recommendations.label: Mild adult typhoid
preferred: Ceftriaxone 2–4 g/day IV divided q12–24h OR cefotaxime 2–6 g/day IV divided q8–12h
alternative: Ciprofloxacin or azithromycin only according to susceptibility/result and source pathway
recommendations.duration: Minimum 7–14 days; IV→PO when improving and an active oral option is available.

recommendations.label: XDR / resistant severe disease
preferred: Meropenem 1 g IV q8h in the NAG XDR pathway
alternative: Use susceptibility and ID/microbiology guidance.
recommendations.duration: Source-/response-specific; verify live NAG.

conditions.diseaseMechanism: Infection causes tissue injury through organism-specific invasion/toxin effects and the host inflammatory response; severity depends on pathogen, site, inoculum, source control and host reserve.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Blood culture is preferred early; stool/urine cultures may become positive later. Susceptibility is important where resistance is prevalent.

conditions.name: Uncomplicated Lower Urinary Tract Infection
conditions.summary: Use a lower-tract regimen guided by current NAG/local susceptibility and avoid agents that do not achieve appropriate urinary activity.
before: Confirm lower-tract symptoms without systemic/upper-tract features
Check pregnancy status, renal function and prior resistant urine cultures

recommendations.label: Uncomplicated cystitis
preferred: Nitrofurantoin or other NAG-listed lower-tract agent based on current local pathway
alternative: Fosfomycin 3 g PO single dose in selected patients; reliability is mainly for E. coli in this context
recommendations.duration: Agent-specific; check latest NAG UTI page.

why: Lower-tract therapy should not be extrapolated to pyelonephritis or systemic infection.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Most bacterial urinary infections ascend from periurethral flora; obstruction, instrumentation, stones and prostate involvement can promote persistence, bacteraemia and sepsis.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Urinalysis and urine culture should be obtained before antibiotics when systemic/complicated infection is suspected.
Obtain blood cultures in sepsis/systemic illness and evaluate obstruction, stones, catheter or abscess where relevant.

conditions.name: Urosepsis
conditions.summary: Treat sepsis and assess for obstructed infected urinary tract, which requires urgent source control.
before: Blood cultures and urine culture
Assess urinary obstruction/stone and need for urgent drainage
Review previous urinary isolates and ESBL/CRE risk
Check renal function

recommendations.label: Local empirical regimen
preferred: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q8h
alternative: Cefepime 1 g IV q8h
recommendations.duration: 10–14 days in the source

recommendations.label: Without shock
preferred: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h OR cefotaxime 2 g IV q8h
alternative: Ceftazidime 2 g IV q8h OR cefepime 2 g IV q8h
recommendations.duration: ≥7 days; early urinary source control is a core treatment principle.

recommendations.label: With shock
preferred: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6–8h
alternative: Meropenem 1 g IV q8h OR imipenem 500 mg IV q6h
recommendations.duration: ≥7 days; choose according to severity, resistance risk and local antibiogram, with early source control.

conditions.diseaseMechanism: Most bacterial urinary infections ascend from periurethral flora; obstruction, instrumentation, stones and prostate involvement can promote persistence, bacteraemia and sepsis.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Urinalysis and urine culture should be obtained before antibiotics when systemic/complicated infection is suspected.
Obtain blood cultures in sepsis/systemic illness and evaluate obstruction, stones, catheter or abscess where relevant.

sourceReconciliation.title: Urosepsis — local empirical table vs current NAG shock stratification
sourceReconciliation.summary: HPUSM lists a local piperacillin/tazobactam empirical regimen, whereas current NAG distinguishes urosepsis without shock from urosepsis with shock and emphasizes obstruction/source control.
points: Do not hide the difference: present HPUSM and NAG regimens side-by-side.
For obstructed infected urinary tract, antimicrobial selection does not replace urgent source control.
Previous urinary isolates, ESBL/CRE risk and renal function can change the targeted and patient-specific regimen.

conditions.name: Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia
conditions.summary: Current NAG paediatric pathway keeps anti-pseudomonal β-lactam monotherapy first-line and warns not to escalate solely because fever persists.
before: Confirm current weight, age/gestation/postmenstrual age, renal function, allergy and microbiology before dosing
Use culture results and local paediatric/NICU epidemiology to narrow therapy
Check the live NAG page because the national guideline is online-only and periodically updated
Obtain cultures promptly and assess haemodynamic stability and focal source

recommendations.label: First line
preferred: Cefepime 50 mg/kg/dose IV q8h (max 6 g/day)
alternative: Piperacillin–tazobactam 300–400 mg/kg/day IV in 4 divided doses (max 16 g/day piperacillin component)
recommendations.duration: Individualise to clinical/microbiological course and neutrophil recovery.

recommendations.label: Unstable / escalation clinically indicated
preferred: Meropenem 60–120 mg/kg/day IV in 3 divided doses (max 6 g/day); may add vancomycin 60 mg/kg/day in 3–4 divided doses (max 2 g/day) for defined indications
alternative: Do not modify initial coverage based solely on persistence of fever.
recommendations.duration: Reassess and de-escalate; discontinue unnecessary double coverage when there is no microbiologic indication.

why: NAG states no clinical advantage for routine β-lactam + aminoglycoside combination in this first-line context.
Vancomycin should be tied to a defined Gram-positive indication rather than added routinely.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Neutropenia reduces innate antibacterial defence, permitting rapid invasive infection with limited inflammatory signs; gut, skin and catheter flora are important portals.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Blood cultures are central before treatment when this does not delay urgent therapy.
Investigate focal symptoms and device sources; interpret cultures with local oncology/haematology epidemiology.

conditions.name: Paediatric Bacterial Meningitis
conditions.summary: Age-specific bacterial meningitis pathway with high-dose CNS β-lactams and organism-directed de-escalation.
before: Confirm current weight, age/gestation/postmenstrual age, renal function, allergy and microbiology before dosing
Use culture results and local paediatric/NICU epidemiology to narrow therapy
Check the live NAG page because the national guideline is online-only and periodically updated
Obtain blood cultures and CSF when safe, without delaying urgent antimicrobial therapy

recommendations.label: Empirical treatment
preferred: Cefotaxime 200–300 mg/kg/day IV in 4 divided doses (max 2 g/dose) OR ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day IV in 2 divided doses (max 2 g/dose; 4 g/day)
alternative: Below 3 months, cefotaxime is preferred; consider adding benzylpenicillin while awaiting cultures because GBS remains important.
recommendations.duration: Organism-specific once identified.

why: CNS infection requires meningitis-specific dosing rather than routine systemic doses.
Below 3 months, NAG prefers cefotaxime because of calcium-containing infusion interaction and bilirubin-displacement concerns with ceftriaxone.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Bloodstream invasion and penetration of the blood–brain barrier trigger meningeal inflammation, cerebral oedema and neurological injury.
diagnosticMicrobiology: CSF cell count, chemistry, microscopy/culture and molecular testing where available; obtain blood cultures.
Use organism/MIC-specific therapy once microbiology is known.

conditions.name: Neonatal Meningitis
conditions.summary: Current NAG neonatal meningitis pathway explicitly separates gestational/postnatal-age dosing and severe hospital-acquired CNS infection.
before: Confirm current weight, age/gestation/postmenstrual age, renal function, allergy and microbiology before dosing
Use culture results and local paediatric/NICU epidemiology to narrow therapy
Check the live NAG page because the national guideline is online-only and periodically updated
Record gestational age, postnatal age and current renal function before interpreting neonatal intervals

recommendations.label: Empirical neonatal meningitis
preferred: Benzylpenicillin 150,000 units/kg/dose with GA/PNA-specific interval OR ampicillin 200–300 mg/kg/day (≤1 week) / 300 mg/kg/day (>1 week), PLUS cefotaxime 50 mg/kg/dose with age-specific interval
alternative: Cefepime 50 mg/kg/dose IV q12h
Severe hospital-acquired CNS infection: meropenem 40 mg/kg/dose with gestation/postnatal-age interval
recommendations.duration: Adjust agent and duration once cultures are known; organism-specific durations supersede.

why: Neonatal clearance changes rapidly with gestation and postnatal age.
GBS, E. coli, Listeria and other Gram-negative bacilli drive empirical coverage.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Perinatal or nosocomial bloodstream infection can seed the meninges; immature immune and blood–brain barrier physiology increases invasive disease risk.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Blood and CSF cultures are essential where feasible; adjust therapy when the organism and susceptibility are known.

conditions.name: Neonatal Necrotising Enterocolitis (NEC)
conditions.summary: NAG provides stage-linked empirical regimens while explicitly noting limited evidence for duration and the need to adapt to culture results.
before: Confirm current weight, age/gestation/postmenstrual age, renal function, allergy and microbiology before dosing
Use culture results and local paediatric/NICU epidemiology to narrow therapy
Check the live NAG page because the national guideline is online-only and periodically updated
Stage NEC clinically/radiologically and involve neonatal surgical team/source control when indicated

recommendations.label: Stage 1
preferred: Ampicillin 100 mg/kg/dose IV with age-specific interval + gentamicin 5 mg/kg/dose OR amikacin 15 mg/kg/dose with CGA-specific interval + metronidazole (15 mg/kg load then gestation-specific maintenance)
alternative: Piperacillin–tazobactam only after recent exposure to first-line antibiotics; PMA-specific interval.
recommendations.duration: Empirical; culture and clinical course guide duration.

recommendations.label: Stage 2 / 3
preferred: Cefotaxime 50 mg/kg/dose IV with age-specific interval + metronidazole neonatal regimen
alternative: Piperacillin–tazobactam only in the source-defined context after recent first-line exposure.
recommendations.duration: NAG lists 10–14 days for the cited Stage 2/3 regimen.

why: NEC is polymicrobial/enteric and treatment includes bowel rest, supportive care and surgical/source-control assessment; antibiotics are only one component.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Prematurity-related intestinal immaturity, dysbiosis, inflammation and mucosal barrier failure can progress to intestinal necrosis and bacterial translocation.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Blood cultures are relevant in systemic illness; bowel disease is usually diagnosed clinically/radiographically rather than by a single culture.

conditions.name: Neonatal Early-Onset Sepsis (<48 h)
conditions.summary: Current NAG EOS regimen uses a GBS/Listeria/Gram-negative strategy with GA/PNA/CGA-specific intervals.
before: Confirm current weight, age/gestation/postmenstrual age, renal function, allergy and microbiology before dosing
Use culture results and local paediatric/NICU epidemiology to narrow therapy
Check the live NAG page because the national guideline is online-only and periodically updated
Obtain blood culture before therapy when feasible and reassess at 36–48 h if cultures remain negative and clinical suspicion is low

recommendations.label: Empirical EOS
preferred: Benzylpenicillin 100,000 units/kg/dose IV with GA/PNA-specific interval OR ampicillin 200–300 mg/kg/day IV age-divided, PLUS gentamicin 5 mg/kg/dose IV with CGA-specific interval
recommendations.duration: Consider stopping at 36–48 h if cultures are negative, initial suspicion was not strong and the baby is reassuring; longer courses depend on culture/clinical syndrome.

why: This source pathway explicitly states meningitis is not assumed in the basic EOS empirical regimen; evaluate separately when meningitis is suspected.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Vertically acquired maternal genital/GI organisms or peripartum exposure can cause rapidly invasive bloodstream infection in the first two days of life.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Blood culture is central; interpret CRP/clinical trajectory as supportive rather than a substitute for culture.

conditions.name: Neonatal Late-Onset Sepsis (>48 h)
conditions.summary: NAG LOS therapy prioritises staphylococci/CoNS while requiring local NICU Gram-negative resistance data for second-line selection.
before: Confirm current weight, age/gestation/postmenstrual age, renal function, allergy and microbiology before dosing
Use culture results and local paediatric/NICU epidemiology to narrow therapy
Check the live NAG page because the national guideline is online-only and periodically updated
Assess central lines/device source and local NICU antibiogram

recommendations.label: First line
preferred: Cloxacillin 50 mg/kg/dose IV with age-specific interval + gentamicin 5 mg/kg/dose IV with CGA-specific interval
alternative: Amikacin may replace gentamicin using NAG CGA-specific interval when appropriate.
recommendations.duration: If positive culture or strong clinical suspicion with negative culture, NAG notes 7 days may be used; extend according to site/pathogen/recovery.

recommendations.label: Second line / resistant Gram-negative context
preferred: Piperacillin–tazobactam with PMA-specific interval
alternative: Cefepime: <28 days 30 mg/kg/dose q12h; >28 days 50 mg/kg/dose q12h.
recommendations.duration: Culture- and site-directed.

why: Premature neonates and those with central catheters commonly have CoNS/staphylococcal LOS; NAG stresses local epidemiology for inducible β-lactamase and ESBL Gram-negative organisms.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: After 48 h, healthcare exposure, vascular access, skin flora and NICU environmental/enteric Gram-negative organisms become increasingly important.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain blood cultures; evaluate central-line/device infection and use local NICU resistance patterns to guide escalation.

conditions.name: Paediatric Acute Pyelonephritis
conditions.summary: Current NAG stratifies treatment by age, with neonatal/young-infant IV therapy and culture-directed oral/IV options in older children.
before: Confirm current weight, age/gestation/postmenstrual age, renal function, allergy and microbiology before dosing
Use culture results and local paediatric/NICU epidemiology to narrow therapy
Check the live NAG page because the national guideline is online-only and periodically updated
Obtain urinalysis and urine culture before antibiotics when feasible
Assess for obstruction/structural urinary abnormality in severe or recurrent infection

recommendations.label: Age 0–2 months
preferred: Ampicillin 50 mg/kg/dose IV (≤1 week q12h; >1 week q8h) + gentamicin 5 mg/kg/dose with CGA-specific interval
alternative: Cefotaxime 150–200 mg/kg/day IV in 3 divided doses (max 6 g/day), may add amikacin 15 mg/kg/dose IV daily
recommendations.duration: 7–10 days; adjust to culture.

recommendations.label: Age ≥3 months
preferred: Cephalexin 25–50 mg/kg/day PO in 2 divided doses (max 2 g/day) OR formulation-specific amoxicillin–clavulanate dosing
alternative: Cefotaxime 150–200 mg/kg/day IV in 3 divided doses OR ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day IV in 1–2 divided doses; may add amikacin in source-defined context
recommendations.duration: 7–10 days; switch to oral when improving and tolerating oral therapy.

why: Age changes likely pathogens, drug handling and acceptable oral/IV strategies; urine culture is essential for narrowing.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Ascending bacterial infection reaches the renal pelvis/parenchyma; younger infants have higher risk of bacteraemia and nonspecific systemic presentation.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain a properly collected urine culture before therapy where possible; blood culture may be appropriate in young/systemically ill infants.

organisms.name: Acinetobacter baumannii
notes: Common ICU healthcare-associated pathogen; colonisation is frequent, so infection-vs-colonisation assessment is essential.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Environmental organism that persists on hospital surfaces and equipment; colonises skin/respiratory tract in some patients.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Low intrinsic virulence but strong environmental persistence, biofilm formation and multidrug resistance permit severe infection in vulnerable ICU hosts.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Distinguish colonisation from true infection; CRAB phenotype drives therapy.
microbiology.morphology: Aerobic, non-fermenting Gram-negative coccobacillus with environmental persistence.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Carbapenem resistance is common in CRAB and often coexists with resistance across multiple antimicrobial classes.

antimicrobialGuide.title: NAG organism antimicrobial quick guide

groups.label: Preferred
groups.text: Cefoperazone/sulbactam in the NAG organism quick guide; use the dedicated CRAB pathway when carbapenem resistant.

groups.label: MDR / CRAB context
groups.text: Open the dedicated CRAB resistance pathway for severity-stratified high-dose sulbactam-based therapy and companion-agent considerations.

antimicrobialGuide.comment: NAG notes that colistin/polymyxin B may have limited clinical efficacy for Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter even when intermediate in vitro activity is reported; when used, combine with one or more active agents and seek ID input.
antimicrobialGuide.guard: Use only as a guideline-linked quick reference. Confirm infection versus colonisation, infection site, phenotype/MIC and isolate-specific susceptibility before definitive therapy.

organisms.name: Burkholderia pseudomallei
notes: Treatment has an intensive phase and prolonged eradication phase.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Soil and surface water in endemic tropical regions; inoculation, inhalation and ingestion are recognised routes.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Facultative intracellular survival, multiple secretion systems and abscess formation allow latent, relapsing and disseminated melioidosis.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Treatment requires intensive and eradication phases; source control and relapse prevention matter.
microbiology.morphology: Slender, motile aerobic Gram-negative bacillus; oxidase positive and able to survive intracellularly.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Intrinsic resistance to many routine agents; ceftazidime or a carbapenem is used for intensive therapy according to melioidosis guidance, followed by eradication therapy.

organisms.name: Candida spp.
notes: Colonisation is common in ICU patients; invasive disease must be distinguished from colonisation.

microbiology.familyOrGroup: Ascomycetous yeasts; family varies by species
microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Normal coloniser of gastrointestinal/skin/mucosal sites; invasive disease follows barrier disruption, broad antibiotics and critical illness.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Adhesion, biofilm formation and host-barrier failure allow candidaemia and deep-seated candidiasis.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Colonisation alone is common in ICU patients and is not equivalent to invasive candidiasis.
microbiology.morphology: Budding yeast; Candida species can form pseudohyphae/hyphae depending on species and conditions.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Species identification and susceptibility matter: non-albicans Candida may have reduced azole susceptibility or intrinsic resistance patterns.

organisms.name: Citrobacter freundii
notes: Moderate/high-risk inducible AmpC organism in the MSIDC consensus.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Gastrointestinal/environmental organism.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Can express inducible chromosomal AmpC, creating clinically significant resistance during therapy.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Moderate/high-risk inducible AmpC organism in MSIDC guidance.
microbiology.morphology: Motile Gram-negative enteric bacillus.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Moderate–high risk inducible AmpC producer; third-generation cephalosporin resistance can emerge during therapy.

organisms.name: Clostridioides difficile
notes: Antibiotic exposure is a major risk; treatment is severity- and recurrence-specific.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Spores persist in healthcare/community environments; colonises the colon after microbiome disruption.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Toxins A/B damage colonic epithelium and drive inflammation, diarrhoea and pseudomembranous colitis.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Do not test/treat asymptomatic colonisation; severity and recurrence history determine therapy.
microbiology.morphology: Anaerobic spore-forming Gram-positive bacillus that produces toxin A/B.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Disease follows microbiome disruption and toxin production; spores persist despite many routine disinfectants, so infection-control measures are critical.

organisms.name: Cryptococcus neoformans
notes: Raised intracranial pressure management is central in cryptococcal meningitis.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Environmental encapsulated yeast; infection follows inhalation with later dissemination, especially in impaired cellular immunity.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Polysaccharide capsule and melanin help evade host defences; CNS tropism produces meningitis and raised intracranial pressure.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Management includes antifungal phases plus aggressive intracranial-pressure assessment/control.
microbiology.morphology: Encapsulated yeast; India ink may demonstrate the capsule but cryptococcal antigen is more sensitive.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Susceptibility testing is selective; induction therapy is driven by CNS/disseminated disease and host immune status.

organisms.name: Enterobacter cloacae complex
notes: MSIDC places Enterobacter cloacae complex among moderate/high-risk inducible AmpC organisms.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Gastrointestinal/environmental organism and healthcare-associated opportunist.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Chromosomal inducible AmpC can be derepressed during β-lactam exposure, producing on-therapy resistance to some cephalosporins.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Moderate/high-risk inducible AmpC organism in MSIDC guidance.
microbiology.morphology: Motile Gram-negative enteric bacilli comprising a species complex.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Moderate–high risk inducible AmpC producer; resistance can emerge with certain β-lactams despite initial in-vitro susceptibility.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Normal gastrointestinal flora; healthcare transmission is important for resistant strains.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Intrinsic and acquired resistance plus tolerance of harsh environments facilitate device, urinary and bloodstream infection in vulnerable hosts.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Species and vancomycin susceptibility matter; E. faecium is generally more resistant than E. faecalis.
microbiology.morphology: Gram-positive cocci in pairs/chains; hardy gastrointestinal commensals.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Intrinsic cephalosporin resistance and acquired vancomycin resistance (VRE) are key therapeutic issues.

antimicrobialGuide.title: NAG organism antimicrobial quick guide

groups.label: Urinary isolate note
groups.text: Nitrofurantoin may be used for susceptible Enterococcus spp. isolated from urine.

antimicrobialGuide.comment: NAG cautions that cephalosporins, aminoglycosides (apart from high-level resistance testing), clindamycin and TMP-SMX can appear active in vitro yet are not clinically effective for Enterococcus.
antimicrobialGuide.guard: Use only as a guideline-linked quick reference. Confirm infection versus colonisation, infection site, phenotype/MIC and isolate-specific susceptibility before definitive therapy.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Normal gastrointestinal flora; extra-intestinal strains cause ascending urinary and invasive infection.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Virulence varies by pathotype; adhesins, capsules, toxins and siderophores contribute to urinary, intestinal and bloodstream disease.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: ESBL and CRE mechanisms can radically change therapy.
microbiology.morphology: Lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod in Enterobacterales; common gut commensal.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: ESBL and carbapenemase acquisition changes treatment; urinary pathotypes possess adhesins that facilitate ascending UTI.

antimicrobialGuide.title: NAG organism antimicrobial quick guide

groups.label: Preferred PO
groups.text: Amoxicillin/clavulanate; ampicillin/sulbactam (sultamicillin where used); cephalexin; cefuroxime; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole

antimicrobialGuide.comment: NAG notes that colistin/polymyxin B may have limited clinical efficacy for Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter even when intermediate in vitro activity is reported; when used, combine with one or more active agents and seek ID input.
antimicrobialGuide.guard: Use only as a guideline-linked quick reference. Confirm infection versus colonisation, infection site, phenotype/MIC and isolate-specific susceptibility before definitive therapy.

organisms.name: Haemophilus influenzae
notes: Common respiratory pathogen; invasive disease and respiratory infection use different dosing contexts.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Human upper respiratory tract; spread by respiratory droplets.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Encapsulated strains evade phagocytosis; non-typeable strains commonly cause mucosal respiratory disease.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: β-lactamase production changes ampicillin/amoxicillin susceptibility.
microbiology.morphology: Small pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacillus requiring X and V growth factors.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: β-lactamase production and PBP changes can confer ampicillin/β-lactam resistance; invasive vs non-typeable strains have different clinical patterns.

antimicrobialGuide.title: NAG organism antimicrobial quick guide
antimicrobialGuide.comment: NAG states that ampicillin susceptibility may be used to predict amoxicillin activity; still interpret the actual isolate and infection site.
antimicrobialGuide.guard: Use only as a guideline-linked quick reference. Confirm infection versus colonisation, infection site, phenotype/MIC and isolate-specific susceptibility before definitive therapy.

organisms.name: Helicobacter pylori
notes: Eradication requires a complete multidrug regimen rather than single-drug therapy.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Human gastric colonisation; transmission is mainly person-to-person.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Urease buffers gastric acid; flagella/mucosal adherence and virulence proteins drive chronic gastritis and ulcer/cancer risk.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Treatment should follow current eradication regimens and local macrolide resistance context.
microbiology.morphology: Curved/spiral, motile Gram-negative bacillus; urease positive and adapted to gastric mucus.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Macrolide/metronidazole resistance can cause eradication failure; regimen selection should reflect current local/national guidance and prior macrolide exposure.

organisms.name: Klebsiella aerogenes
notes: Moderate/high-risk inducible AmpC organism in the MSIDC consensus.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Gastrointestinal/environmental healthcare opportunist.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Inducible chromosomal AmpC can be derepressed after β-lactam exposure.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Moderate/high-risk inducible AmpC organism in MSIDC guidance.
microbiology.morphology: Motile Gram-negative enteric bacillus formerly Enterobacter aerogenes.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Moderate–high risk inducible AmpC producer; cefepime/carbapenem use depends on susceptibility, site and severity.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Gastrointestinal/oropharyngeal colonisation with healthcare spread in high-risk settings.
microbiology.pathogenesis: A prominent polysaccharide capsule, siderophores and hypervirulent clones contribute to invasive disease; ESBL/carbapenemases drive treatment failure.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Ask whether the isolate is ESBL/CRE and, for CRE, whether a carbapenemase/MBL is known.
microbiology.morphology: Encapsulated, lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod in Enterobacterales.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: ESBL and carbapenemases (including NDM/MBL, KPC and OXA-48-like) are clinically important resistance mechanisms.

antimicrobialGuide.title: NAG organism antimicrobial quick guide

groups.label: Preferred PO
groups.text: Amoxicillin/clavulanate; ampicillin/sulbactam (sultamicillin where used); cephalexin; cefuroxime; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole

antimicrobialGuide.comment: NAG notes that colistin/polymyxin B may have limited clinical efficacy for Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter even when intermediate in vitro activity is reported; when used, combine with one or more active agents and seek ID input.
antimicrobialGuide.guard: Use only as a guideline-linked quick reference. Confirm infection versus colonisation, infection site, phenotype/MIC and isolate-specific susceptibility before definitive therapy.

organisms.name: Leptospira spp.
notes: Severe disease may include AKI, pulmonary haemorrhage, shock and arrhythmia.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Animal renal carriage with urine contamination of water/soil; infection follows skin/mucosal exposure.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Spirochaetaemia followed by endothelial/organ injury can produce jaundice, AKI, haemorrhage and pulmonary disease.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Treat compatible severe disease promptly; diagnostic serology may be negative early.
microbiology.morphology: Thin motile spirochaete with hooked ends; pathogenic Leptospira disseminate hematogenously.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Routine susceptibility testing is not used; severity-based penicillin/ceftriaxone or doxycycline regimens are chosen clinically.

organisms.name: Listeria monocytogenes
notes: Consider in older, pregnant and immunocompromised hosts in meningitis pathways.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Food/environmental organism with gastrointestinal entry; higher risk in pregnancy, older adults and impaired cellular immunity.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Intracellular survival and actin-mediated cell-to-cell spread enable CNS and invasive disease.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Cephalosporins are intrinsically ineffective; ampicillin/benzylpenicillin is central in susceptible disease.
microbiology.morphology: Small facultative intracellular Gram-positive rod with tumbling motility.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Cephalosporins are intrinsically inactive; ampicillin/amoxicillin-based therapy is the key treatment implication.

organisms.name: Neisseria meningitidis
notes: Meningococcal disease requires urgent therapy and public-health/contact prophylaxis considerations.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Human nasopharynx; droplet spread and close-contact transmission.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Capsule enables bloodstream survival; endotoxin-driven inflammation can cause fulminant meningococcaemia and shock.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Rapid public-health/contact prophylaxis assessment is part of management.
microbiology.morphology: Encapsulated Gram-negative diplococcus, oxidase positive.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: β-lactam susceptibility can vary; definitive therapy should follow susceptibility and national public-health guidance.

organisms.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii
notes: Host immune status and oxygenation determine treatment intensity and steroid indication.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Human respiratory organism; disease occurs predominantly with impaired cellular immunity.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Alveolar fungal proliferation triggers diffuse interstitial inflammation and severe gas-exchange impairment.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Assess hypoxaemia because adjunctive corticosteroid criteria depend on severity in HIV-associated PJP.
microbiology.morphology: Opportunistic fungus with trophic and cystic forms; diagnosis requires respiratory specimen microscopy/PCR rather than routine culture.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: No routine clinical susceptibility testing; TMP-SMX remains first-line and alternatives are chosen by intolerance/response.

organisms.name: Proteus mirabilis
notes: Common urinary pathogen; resistance phenotype and renal function guide therapy.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Gastrointestinal flora; ascending urinary infection is common.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Strong urease activity alkalinises urine and promotes struvite stone formation and catheter encrustation.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Intrinsic reduced susceptibility to some agents and urinary tract anatomy/stones matter.
microbiology.morphology: Highly motile, swarming, urease-positive Gram-negative enteric bacillus.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Urease promotes alkaline urine/struvite stones; susceptibility-guided therapy is essential because acquired β-lactam and fluoroquinolone resistance occurs.

organisms.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
notes: Expected-spectrum table includes activity from selected antipseudomonal β-lactams and aminoglycosides; susceptibility testing remains decisive.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Soil/water and moist healthcare reservoirs such as sinks and respiratory equipment.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Opportunistic invasion is supported by biofilm/alginate, exotoxin A, endotoxin, secreted enzymes and impaired host defences; resistance often involves permeability/efflux/AmpC mechanisms.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Resistance phenotype matters more than the organism name alone; DTR is a treatment-limiting phenotype.
microbiology.morphology: Aerobic, non-fermenting Gram-negative rod; oxidase positive; forms biofilm.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Intrinsic and acquired mechanisms include low permeability, efflux, inducible/chromosomal AmpC and OprD changes; DTR phenotype should drive treatment selection.

antimicrobialGuide.title: NAG organism antimicrobial quick guide
antimicrobialGuide.comment: NAG notes that colistin/polymyxin B may have limited clinical efficacy for Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter even when intermediate in vitro activity is reported; when used, combine with one or more active agents and seek ID input.
antimicrobialGuide.guard: Use only as a guideline-linked quick reference. Confirm infection versus colonisation, infection site, phenotype/MIC and isolate-specific susceptibility before definitive therapy.

organisms.name: Salmonella Typhi
notes: Travel/geography and susceptibility pattern materially change therapy.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Humans are the reservoir; faeco-oral transmission via contaminated food/water.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Invades intestinal mucosa, survives in macrophages and disseminates through the reticuloendothelial system.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Travel/exposure history and susceptibility are important because fluoroquinolone resistance is common in many regions.
microbiology.morphology: Motile Gram-negative enteric bacillus; typhoidal strain is adapted to humans.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Reduced fluoroquinolone susceptibility and multidrug resistance are clinically important; follow current local/national susceptibility data.

antimicrobialGuide.title: NAG organism antimicrobial quick guide
antimicrobialGuide.comment: Typhoidal Salmonella treatment must follow susceptibility and the syndrome-specific NAG typhoid pathway; resistance patterns can materially change therapy.
antimicrobialGuide.guard: Use only as a guideline-linked quick reference. Confirm infection versus colonisation, infection site, phenotype/MIC and isolate-specific susceptibility before definitive therapy.

organisms.name: Serratia marcescens
notes: MSIDC describes a lower risk of clinically significant inducible AmpC than Enterobacter cloacae complex/K. aerogenes/C. freundii.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Environmental and gastrointestinal organism associated with healthcare reservoirs/devices.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Opportunistic invasion and intrinsic/acquired resistance mechanisms can complicate device and bloodstream infection.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: MSIDC categorises Serratia as lower risk for clinically significant inducible AmpC than Enterobacter cloacae complex/K. aerogenes/C. freundii.
microbiology.morphology: Motile Gram-negative enteric bacillus; may produce prodigiosin pigment.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Can carry inducible AmpC and additional acquired resistance; use isolate susceptibility and site/severity to choose therapy.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Colonises skin and anterior nares; spreads by direct/contact transmission and can seed the bloodstream from skin/device sources.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Adhesins, immune-evasion mechanisms, coagulase and multiple toxins allow abscess formation, tissue injury and metastatic infection.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Persistent S. aureus bacteraemia requires active search for source/metastatic foci; MSSA and MRSA require different definitive therapy.
microbiology.morphology: Gram-positive cocci in clusters; catalase/coagulase positive.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: MRSA expresses altered PBP2a-mediated β-lactam resistance; MSSA should preferentially receive an active antistaphylococcal β-lactam when feasible.

antimicrobialGuide.title: NAG organism antimicrobial quick guide

groups.label: MSSA preferred
groups.text: IV cloxacillin or cefazolin; PO cephalexin or cloxacillin

groups.label: MRSA preferred / alternatives
groups.text: IV vancomycin; alternatives include linezolid and ceftaroline; selected oral combination/CA-MRSA options are phenotype- and syndrome-dependent.

groups.label: CA-MRSA options
groups.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or clindamycin; other source-listed options include linezolid or doxycycline depending on syndrome/susceptibility.

antimicrobialGuide.comment: Methicillin resistance changes the beta-lactam interpretation. Rifampicin should not be used alone for staphylococcal antimicrobial therapy.
antimicrobialGuide.guard: Use only as a guideline-linked quick reference. Confirm infection versus colonisation, infection site, phenotype/MIC and isolate-specific susceptibility before definitive therapy.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Water, sinks, fomites, plants and hospital equipment.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Usually low-virulence/opportunistic; infection occurs in immunocompromised or chronically ill hosts. Intrinsic β-lactam/carbapenem resistance is a major clinical feature.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Many respiratory isolates are colonisers; do not treat colonisation.
microbiology.morphology: Aerobic non-fermenting Gram-negative rod associated with water and healthcare environments.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Intrinsic multidrug resistance includes β-lactamases and efflux; carbapenems are intrinsically ineffective and colonisation is common.

organisms.name: Streptococcus pneumoniae
notes: Major CAP/meningitis pathogen; site-specific breakpoints and CNS dosing matter.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Human nasopharyngeal coloniser transmitted by respiratory droplets.
microbiology.pathogenesis: The polysaccharide capsule is the principal antiphagocytic virulence factor; mucosal barrier disruption allows pneumonia, bacteraemia and meningitis.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Asplenia and impaired humoral immunity increase invasive disease risk.
microbiology.morphology: Lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococcus; alpha-haemolytic and encapsulated.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Capsule is a major virulence determinant; β-lactam susceptibility varies and site-specific breakpoints matter, especially in meningitis.

antimicrobialGuide.title: NAG organism antimicrobial quick guide
antimicrobialGuide.comment: For non-meningitis isolates, NAG describes additional agents whose activity may be inferred from penicillin susceptibility. Meningitis uses separate MIC breakpoints and syndrome-specific therapy.
antimicrobialGuide.guard: Use only as a guideline-linked quick reference. Confirm infection versus colonisation, infection site, phenotype/MIC and isolate-specific susceptibility before definitive therapy.

organisms.name: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus)
phenotypes: Usually β-lactam susceptible; susceptibility testing matters for alternatives
notes: Major vertically acquired neonatal pathogen; source-specific high-dose penicillin/ampicillin schedules vary by sepsis vs meningitis.

microbiology.morphology: Gram-positive cocci in chains; beta-haemolytic streptococcus.
microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Commonly colonises maternal gastrointestinal/genitourinary tract; vertical transmission can occur around labour/delivery.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Capsular polysaccharide and other surface factors support immune evasion and invasive bloodstream/CNS disease, particularly in neonates.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Penicillin/ampicillin remain core therapies in the cited NAG neonatal pathways; macrolide/clindamycin resistance can limit alternatives and should be susceptibility-guided.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: In neonatal disease, sepsis and meningitis use different source-specific penicillin exposure; do not reuse a sepsis dose for meningitis.

antimicrobialGuide.title: NAG organism antimicrobial quick guide
antimicrobialGuide.comment: This quick guide covers Group B Streptococcus together with other beta-haemolytic streptococci; syndrome-specific therapy and susceptibility still apply.
antimicrobialGuide.guard: Use only as a guideline-linked quick reference. Confirm infection versus colonisation, infection site, phenotype/MIC and isolate-specific susceptibility before definitive therapy.

organisms.name: Coagulase-Negative Staphylococci (CoNS)
notes: Skin commensals can be contaminants, colonisers or true device-associated pathogens; interpretation depends on clinical context and repeated/paired cultures.

microbiology.morphology: Gram-positive cocci in clusters; catalase positive and coagulase negative.
microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Normal skin flora; healthcare-associated infection is strongly linked to intravascular catheters, prosthetic material and biofilm.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Adhesion to foreign material and biofilm formation permit persistence on devices with reduced host clearance and antimicrobial penetration.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Methicillin resistance is common in healthcare-associated CoNS; definitive treatment should follow species/susceptibility and determine whether a positive culture represents contamination or true infection.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: A single positive culture may be contamination; multiple concordant cultures plus compatible clinical/device findings increase the likelihood of true infection.
