resistance.name: AmpC β-Lactamase-Producing Enterobacterales
resistance.summary: AmpC risk changes interpretation of β-lactam susceptibility. Site and susceptibility determine whether cefepime or a carbapenem is preferred.

sourceCards.title: Moderate inducible AmpC risk — urinary tract
sourceCards.text: Uncomplicated cystitis: use a susceptible lower-tract option such as nitrofurantoin/TMP-SMX or a single aminoglycoside; pyelonephritis/cUTI: TMP-SMX, once-daily aminoglycoside with TDM, or cefepime are source-listed options.
bullets: Confirm susceptibility before choosing definitive therapy.
Fluoroquinolone is a less-preferred option when susceptible.

sourceCards.title: Outside urinary tract
sourceCards.text: Cefepime is a key preferred option when susceptible; high-inoculum/severe disease and reduced cefepime susceptibility may shift therapy toward a carbapenem.
bullets: Piperacillin–tazobactam is not recommended for moderate/high-risk inducible AmpC organisms in the dedicated consensus.

resistance.name: Carbapenem-Resistant Acinetobacter baumannii
resistance.summary: CRAB treatment starts with infection-versus-colonisation assessment, then uses severity, ampicillin-sulbactam susceptibility, infection site and full susceptibility data. Malaysian HPUSM/MSIDC guidance places high-dose sulbactam-based therapy at the centre of many true-infection regimens.

sourceCards.title: HPUSM CRAB — severity and susceptibility stratification
sourceCards.text: Local targeted guidance separates mild infection from moderate–severe disease and also distinguishes ampicillin-sulbactam susceptible versus non-susceptible mild CRAB.
bullets: Mild + susceptible: ampicillin/sulbactam 3 g IV q4h.
Mild + non-susceptible: high-dose ampicillin/sulbactam 9 g IV q8h.
Moderate–severe: ampicillin/sulbactam 9 g IV q8h infused over 3 h, with or without meropenem 2 g IV q8h infused over 3 h according to the local pathway/authorisation requirements.
Local table duration: 7–10 days; individualise by site, source control and response.

sourceCards.title: MSIDC CRAB — core treatment principles
sourceCards.text: Do not treat colonisation. For true CRAB infection, MSIDC uses sulbactam-based therapy with dose intensity and combination strategy determined by severity and susceptibility.
bullets: Mild + ampicillin-sulbactam susceptible: ampicillin/sulbactam providing 6 g sulbactam/day may be used as monotherapy.

Mild + non-susceptible: ampicillin/sulbactam providing 9 g sulbactam/day plus minocycline or polymyxin B; colistin may be used if polymyxin B is unavailable and is preferred for UTI because of urinary exposure.
Moderate–severe: combination therapy centred on ampicillin/sulbactam providing 9 g sulbactam/day plus minocycline or polymyxin B.
Minocycline has low serum/urinary concentrations; site matters.

sourceCards.title: HPUSM sulbactam preparation / renal table
sourceCards.text: The local appendix gives practical formulation, renal/RRT, dilution and infusion instructions for high-dose sulbactam regimens.
bullets: Unasyn 1.5 g/vial contains ampicillin 1 g + sulbactam 0.5 g (1:0.5).
Sulperazone 1 g/vial contains cefoperazone 500 mg + sulbactam 500 mg (1:1).
Target sulbactam/day in the local table: CrCl >50: 9 g/day; CrCl 20–50: 6 g/day; CrCl <20/HD: 4 g/day; CVVH/CVVHD/CVVHDF: 9 g/day.
Dilute in 100 mL; compatible diluents listed locally include water for injection, 0.9% sodium chloride and 5% dextrose; infuse over 4 h.

sourceCards.title: MSIDC CRAB — companion agents / cautions
sourceCards.text: The dedicated MDR guideline adds site-specific polymyxin considerations and cautions against several low-value combinations.
bullets: Polymyxin B is generally preferred over colistin outside UTI; colistin is preferred for UTI because CMS renal elimination can produce higher urinary exposure.
Cefiderocol may be considered for CRAB, preferably combined with high-dose ampicillin/sulbactam in the cited guidance.
Nebulised antibiotics are not routinely recommended for CRAB.
Meropenem + colistin has not demonstrated superiority to colistin monotherapy in cited trials; avoid routine triple meropenem + polymyxin + ampicillin/sulbactam because of toxicity/limited benefit.

sulbactamGuide.title: Dosage regimen of sulbactam for Acinetobacter MDR
formulations: Unasyn 1.5 g/vial = ampicillin 1 g + sulbactam 0.5 g (ratio 1:0.5).
Sulperazone 1 g/vial = cefoperazone 500 mg + sulbactam 500 mg (ratio 1:1).
administration: Listed compatible diluents: water for injection, 0.9% sodium chloride or 5% dextrose.
precautions: High-dose Unasyn can produce substantial sodium exposure; the local guide gives an example of 9 g q8h providing about 90 mmol sodium/day. Monitor for hypernatraemia and excess sodium/fluid load; monitor sodium/fluid balance and consider a lower-sodium diluent strategy where appropriate and compatible.

High-dose cefoperazone/sulbactam may contribute to vitamin-K deficiency/hypoprothrombinaemia; monitor haematologic/coagulation parameters where clinically indicated and follow local specialist/pharmacy guidance.

resistance.name: Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacterales
resistance.summary: CRE is heterogeneous. Determine whether carbapenemase is present and identify the enzyme (e.g. NDM/MBL, KPC, OXA-48-like) because this can change active options.

sourceCards.title: Non-CP CRE with retained meropenem/imipenem susceptibility
sourceCards.text: Use high-dose meropenem or imipenem with 3–4 h extended infusion when the source MIC criteria are satisfied.

sourceCards.title: CRE outside urinary tract — ceftazidime/avibactam susceptible
sourceCards.text: Ceftazidime–avibactam is preferred. Cefiderocol, high-dose tigecycline or polymyxin B are less-preferred source-listed alternatives; combination strategies are reserved for selected severe/high-burden scenarios.

sourceCards.title: Presumed/confirmed NDM
sourceCards.text: Preferred: ceftazidime–avibactam PLUS aztreonam administered simultaneously, OR cefiderocol.
bullets: Consider high-dose extended-infusion meropenem as a companion only when MIC ≤8 mg/L in the source-defined combination context.

resistance.name: ESBL-Producing Enterobacterales
resistance.summary: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase phenotype. Treatment depends on infection site, severity and susceptibility; avoid treating the resistance label without the clinical syndrome.

sourceCards.title: Local severe/critical illness signal
sourceCards.text: HPUSM uses ertapenem for selected severe ESBL infection and meropenem/imipenem for critically ill/intubated ICU patients; hypoalbuminaemia and infection site alter the choice.

sourceCards.title: Uncomplicated cystitis / pyelonephritis-cUTI
sourceCards.text: Use susceptible oral/lower-tract options for uncomplicated cystitis; for pyelonephritis/cUTI, TMP-SMX or ciprofloxacin are preferred when susceptible, with aminoglycoside/carbapenem alternatives in selected cases.
bullets: Avoid unnecessary carbapenem exposure when a reliable active narrower option exists.

sourceCards.title: Infection outside urinary tract
sourceCards.text: Carbapenem is the preferred class in the dedicated MSIDC guidance; in critically ill patients or marked hypoalbuminaemia, meropenem/imipenem is favoured over ertapenem.
bullets: Piperacillin–tazobactam and cefepime are not recommended as definitive ESBL therapy outside narrow exceptions described in the source.

resistance.name: KPC-Producing CRE
resistance.summary: Carbapenemase-producing CRE with a serine carbapenemase mechanism. Therapy should be susceptibility- and site-directed using dedicated CRE guidance.

sourceCards.title: If ceftazidime–avibactam susceptible
sourceCards.text: For CRE infection outside the urinary tract, MSIDC lists ceftazidime–avibactam as the preferred option when susceptible.
bullets: Confirm susceptibility and infection site.
Use ID/clinical microbiology review for severe/high-burden infection.

resistance.name: MDR / DTR Pseudomonas aeruginosa
resistance.summary: Use site, severity and in-vitro activity. DTR Pseudomonas should trigger dedicated MDR guidance rather than automatic carbapenem escalation.

sourceCards.title: MDR Pseudomonas, carbapenem non-susceptible but traditional β-lactam susceptible
sourceCards.text: Prefer susceptible ceftazidime, cefepime or piperacillin–tazobactam using high-dose extended infusion.

sourceCards.title: DTR Pseudomonas — cystitis / cUTI
sourceCards.text: Preferred newer β-lactams are ceftolozane–tazobactam or ceftazidime–avibactam when susceptible; site-specific alternatives include amikacin, colistin or cefiderocol.

sourceCards.title: DTR Pseudomonas — infection outside urinary tract
sourceCards.text: Prefer ceftolozane–tazobactam or ceftazidime–avibactam. Cefiderocol or polymyxin B + a second susceptible agent are less-preferred source options.
bullets: MSIDC does not recommend routine combination therapy when an optimal active agent is available.
Nebulised antibiotics are not recommended in the cited respiratory DTR-Pseudomonas guidance.

resistance.name: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus
resistance.summary: MRSA is resistant to usual antistaphylococcal β-lactams because of altered PBP2a. Use local MRSA risk/prevalence and syndrome severity to decide empirical coverage.

sourceCards.title: Local guidance
sourceCards.text: HPUSM recommends vancomycin for empirical therapy when MRSA risk is high/severe and for confirmed MRSA; it states vancomycin is inferior to cloxacillin for MSSA.

resistance.name: Methicillin-Susceptible Staphylococcus aureus
resistance.summary: HPUSM notes MSSA causes community and hospital-acquired bloodstream/invasive infection and that vancomycin is inferior to anti-staphylococcal penicillins such as cloxacillin for MSSA.

sourceCards.title: Local HPUSM principle
sourceCards.text: Use an anti-staphylococcal penicillin such as cloxacillin for susceptible S. aureus rather than continuing vancomycin solely for convenience; complicated MSSA infection warrants ID consultation.

resistance.name: NDM / Metallo-β-Lactamase Producing CRE
resistance.summary: Metallo-β-lactamase-producing CRE require a different strategy from KPC/OXA-48-like disease because avibactam does not inhibit the MBL itself.

sourceCards.title: Presumed/confirmed NDM — infection outside urinary tract
sourceCards.text: MSIDC lists ceftazidime–avibactam PLUS aztreonam given simultaneously as a preferred regimen, or cefiderocol as another preferred option.
bullets: Tigecycline high dose or polymyxin B are less-preferred alternatives in the source.
Avoid high-dose tigecycline for bacteraemia in the cited pathway.

resistance.name: Non-Carbapenemase-Producing CRE
resistance.summary: CRE can result from non-carbapenemase β-lactamase activity plus permeability changes. Some isolates remain susceptible to meropenem/imipenem despite ertapenem resistance.

sourceCards.title: Meropenem/imipenem susceptible non-CP CRE
sourceCards.text: If meropenem and imipenem MICs remain ≤1 µg/mL with ertapenem non-susceptibility, MSIDC recommends high-dose meropenem or imipenem using 3–4 h extended infusion.

resistance.name: OXA-48-like CRE
resistance.summary: OXA-48-like carbapenemase phenotype. Use susceptibility testing and the CRE pathway rather than assuming all carbapenems or β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitors behave alike.

sourceCards.title: CRE mechanism-directed approach
sourceCards.text: MSIDC separates carbapenemase-producing CRE by mechanism and ceftazidime–avibactam susceptibility; use the CRE treatment algorithm and AST.

resistance.name: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia
resistance.summary: Intrinsically resistant to carbapenems. Distinguish colonisation from infection and use susceptibility/site/severity to select therapy.

sourceCards.title: First question: infection or colonisation?
sourceCards.text: If the isolate represents colonisation, do not treat.

sourceCards.title: Treatment when true infection is present
sourceCards.text: TMP-SMX IV/PO is preferred. Cefiderocol or ceftazidime–avibactam PLUS aztreonam are less-preferred source-listed options.
bullets: For moderate–severe infection, the source prefers combination therapy when using TMP-SMX or cefiderocol until clinical improvement.
Levofloxacin or minocycline may serve as a susceptibility-directed companion.

sourceCards.title: Tetracycline caveat
sourceCards.text: Because minocycline/tetracycline derivatives have low urine and serum concentrations, avoid them for UTI and use only in combination for bacteraemia.

checklist: Blood pressure stable with no unexplained hypotension
Functional gastrointestinal tract; oral fluids/food tolerated (NAG example: ≥1 L/day oral fluid or ≥40 mL/h enteral nutrition)
No vomiting, significant diarrhoea, malabsorptive disorder, short-bowel syndrome or swallowing disorder compromising oral absorption
An appropriate oral antimicrobial is available after considering bioavailability, interactions and allergy
No infection/source/device reason requiring continued IV therapy
Culture/susceptibility and total treatment duration/stop date reviewed
avoid: Bone and joint infection during the early phase
Undrained or inadequately drained deep abscess
Cystic-fibrosis/bronchiectasis exacerbation when prolonged IV therapy is required
High-risk neutropenia or severe infection during chemotherapy-related neutropenia
Melioidosis before at least 14 days of IV therapy
Septicaemia/critical infection with high mortality risk
Severe soft-tissue infection such as necrotising fasciitis or invasive Group A Streptococcus
Severely immunocompromised patient such as solid-organ or bone-marrow transplant when IV therapy remains required
notes: NAG states that liver abscess, adequately drained abscess/empyema, osteomyelitis and septic arthritis may be changed to oral therapy after ≥2 weeks IV in appropriate improving patients.

hypoalbuminaemia.name: Hypoalbuminaemia (albumin ≤25 g/L)
hypoalbuminaemia.summary: Highly protein-bound antimicrobials may have increased free fraction, volume of distribution and clearance, reducing exposure despite a higher unbound fraction.
principles: Avoid ertapenem in critically ill patients with marked hypoalbuminaemia in the cited MSIC appendix.
Use drug-specific loading/maintenance or TDM strategies rather than reducing dose solely because albumin is low.

obesity.name: Obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²)
obesity.summary: Dosing weight depends on antimicrobial properties. Volume of distribution informs loading dose; clearance informs maintenance dose.
principles: Drug-specific obesity recommendations should supersede generic weight rules.

ecmo.name: ECMO
ecmo.summary: ECMO can alter antimicrobial pharmacokinetics through circuit sequestration, haemodilution, altered volume of distribution and drug elimination; available antibiotic dosing data are limited.
principles: Use standard/critical-illness loading exposure unless a drug-specific source states otherwise.
Prioritise TDM when available for narrow-therapeutic-index agents.

augmented-renal-clearance.name: Augmented renal clearance (ARC)
augmented-renal-clearance.summary: Critical illness can produce renal clearance above normal, risking subtherapeutic exposure for renally eliminated antimicrobials.
principles: Use measured/estimated clearance and clinical context rather than assuming normal exposure at a “normal” creatinine.
MSIDC cefiderocol table includes a higher-frequency regimen for CrCl >120 mL/min.

cns-infection.name: Central nervous system infection
cns-infection.summary: CNS infection may require higher β-lactam exposure than non-CNS infection. The MSIC renal table explicitly provides high-dose meropenem and higher-dose cefepime/ceftazidime contexts.
principles: Do not apply a standard non-CNS dose to meningitis/ventriculitis without checking the syndrome-specific source.
Renal adjustment must preserve adequate CNS exposure while reducing toxicity risk.

sources.summary: NAG: AUC/MIC is the efficacy exposure metric; TDM is indicated when vancomycin is expected for >48 h, with more frequent monitoring when PK is unstable.
MSIC provides loading, renal/RRT regimens and sampling schedules; its ICU appendix lists AUC24/MIC target 400–600.

aucMethods: Bayesian software is described by NAG as the gold-standard estimation method.
An alternative NAG approach uses two concentrations (peak and trough) with analytic PK equations.
vancomycin.monitoringIndication: NAG: TDM for all patients expected to receive vancomycin for >48 h.
vancomycin.monitoringFrequency: NAG: at least biweekly in clinically stable patients; more frequent monitoring when pharmacokinetics are changing/unstable.
vancomycin.msicTarget: MSIC ICU appendix: AUC0-24/MIC target 400–600; infusion rate should not exceed 10 mg/min in its hypoalbuminaemia table.

msicSampling.normalRenal: Initial pre-level 30 min before the 4th dose and post-level 1 h after completion of the 4th dose in the cited MSIC approach.
msicSampling.crcl30to50: Initial assay 24 h after first maintenance dose.
msicSampling.crclBelow30: Initial assay 24 h after loading dose; subsequent dosing guided by TDM.
msicSampling.HD: If loading dose before HD, initial level 24 h after supplemental dose; if after HD, 24 h after loading dose.
msicSampling.CRRT: Pre-level 30 min before the second maintenance dose in the cited MSIC CRRT section; maintenance depends on MIC/effluent rate.

vancomycin.status: SOURCE-RECONCILED — NAG/MSIC principles preserved; AbxHub does not include an unvalidated single-level AUC calculator.
nagPaediatric: Neonates: 10–20 mg/kg/dose with interval q8–48h according to postmenstrual age, weight and serum creatinine.
Age 3 months–<12 years: 60–80 mg/kg/day divided; q6h is listed for normal renal function.
Age ≥12 years: 60–70 mg/kg/day divided q6–8h with normal renal function.
Paediatric CNS DRSP pathway lists vancomycin 60 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses with target AUC24 400–600 mg·h/L.

maintenance: 500 mg q12h when susceptible isolate MIC ≤0.5 mg/L
500 mg q8h when MIC ≤1 mg/L and CRRT effluent rate <30 mL/kg/h
1 g q12h when MIC ≤1 mg/L and CRRT effluent rate >30 mL/kg/h
msicCrrtRegimens.sampling: MSIC cited CRRT approach: pre-level/trough 30 min before the second maintenance dose.
msicCrrtRegimens.warning: These are source-specific example regimens, not an automatic dose calculator. Confirm actual CRRT modality/effluent, residual renal function, MIC and TDM.

workflowValidation.status: SOURCE-RECONCILED / PATIENT-SPECIFIC AUC CALCULATION REQUIRES A VALIDATED METHOD
requiredInputs: complete dose history with administration times
serum concentration value(s) with exact sampling times
acceptedSourceMethods: Bayesian AUC estimation (described by NAG as the gold-standard method)
doNotDo: Do not estimate AUC from a single trough using an unvalidated shortcut.
Do not reuse a previous AUC after a major renal/RRT or haemodynamic change without reassessment.

sources.summary: NAG describes extended-interval/single-daily dosing and lists patient groups where it is not appropriate, including pregnancy, CrCl <30 mL/min, dialysis, endocarditis and haemodynamic instability.
MSIC provides timed level sampling for single-daily and conventional aminoglycoside dosing and recommends more frequent monitoring with changing renal function/nephrotoxins.

aminoglycoside.pkpd: Concentration-dependent killing; NAG describes a target peak concept >10× MIC for EID/SDD.

msicSampling.singleDaily: After the 2nd dose: post-dose levels at 2 h and 6 h in the cited MSIC approach.
msicSampling.conventional: Trough 30 min before next dose; peak 30 min after completion of a 30-min infusion.
msicSampling.repeat: At least weekly when stable; more frequently with changing renal function or concurrent nephrotoxins.

aminoglycoside.status: SOURCE-RECONCILED FOR MONITORING PRINCIPLES — population-specific dosing and TDM rules remain separate.
aminoglycoside.nagChildrenMonitoring: NAG: in children, consider both peak and trough when renal function changes acutely or treatment failure is suspected; subsequent monitoring should be considered at least weekly.
aminoglycoside.neonatalGuard: Neonatal NAG CGA/PNA-based gentamicin/amikacin schedules are population-specific and must not be substituted with the adult EID/SDD nomogram.

workflowValidation.status: SOURCE-RECONCILED / NO AUTOMATIC NOMOGRAM REDOSING ENGINE
requiredInputs: serum level value(s) and exact sampling time
routingRules: If a NAG EID/SDD exclusion is present, do not apply a routine extended-interval nomogram.
Neonatal CGA/PNA schedules are a separate population pathway.
Gram-positive synergy dosing has different targets/monitoring from Gram-negative treatment dosing.
futureOptionalIntegration: validated aminoglycoside nomogram or PK service integration

records.name: Acyclovir
records.quickDose: NAG suspected HSV encephalitis: 10 mg/kg IV q8h; treatment duration commonly 14–21 days.
records.blueBookDose:
ADULT: 5 mg/kg by IV infusion 8 hourly for 5 days, doubled to 10mg/kg every 8 hourly in varicella-zoster in the immunocompromised and in simplex encephalitis (usually given for at least 10 days in encephalitis; possibly for 14 - 21 days). 

NEONATE & INFANT up to 3 months with disseminated herpes simplex: 20mg/kg every 8 hourly for 14 days (21 days in CNS involvement), varicella-zoster 10-20mg/kg every 8 hourly usually for 7 days. 

CHILD, 3 months - 12 years: Herpes simplex or Varicella Zoster: 250 mg/m2 8 hourly for 5 days, doubled to 500 mg/m2 8 hourly for varicella-zoster in the immunocompromised and in simplex encephalitis (usually given for 10 days in encephalitis) | Indication (i)
Treatment for Herpes Simplex: ADULT - 200mg 5 times daily; In severely immune-compromised patients: dose can be doubled to 400 mg. CHILD - two years and above should be given adult dosages, infants and children below two years old should be given half the adult dose.

Treatment for Varicella Zoster: ADULT - 800mg 5 times daily; CHILD - 6 years and over: 800 mg four times daily, 2 - < 6 years: 400 mg four times daily, Under 2 years: 200 mg four times daily.

Indication (ii)
ADULT - Immune-compromised patients: 200 mg four times daily. Severely immune-compromised patients: dose can be doubled to 400 mg.
CHILD - two years and above should be given adult dosages, infants and children below two years old should be given half the adult dose.

Dosing is according to Product Information Leaflet.

Children and adults (including elderly): 
Up to 60kg: 50,000 units/kg/day to a maximum of 75,000 units/kg/day. The total daily dose should be divided into three doses given at approximately 8-hour intervals.

- Mild (CrCl 20-50 ml/min): 1-2 million units every 8 hr. 
- Moderate (CrCl 10-20 ml/min): 1 million units every 12-18 hr. 
- Severe (CrCl <10 ml/min): 1 million units every 18-24 hr.

highRiskRRT.policy: AbxHub applies an RRT regimen only when it is explicitly structured in the cited source. Modality, effluent rate, residual renal function, infection site/severity and TDM can materially change exposure; when the source does not provide a regimen, AbxHub does not extrapolate one.

highRiskRRT.effluentRateRule: CRRT is not a single dose category. Where a source gives modality/effluent-specific dosing (for example vancomycin), AbxHub shows it explicitly. Where the source does not provide a validated CRRT regimen, AbxHub displays a guard rather than extrapolating.
principles: Preserve/source-check loading or stat doses in critical illness; maintenance adjustment is a separate step.
Record modality (HD/CVVH/CVVHD/CVVHDF), actual effluent prescription, residual renal function, rapidly changing renal function and TDM availability.
Use concentration-guided redosing for high-risk narrow-therapeutic-index agents when the source requires it.
Do not convert a renal-dose table into a prescription without indication/site/MIC context.
